editorials.title: Ground control: On ISRO, policy and and its focus
editorials.passage:
The irony was evident: on the day the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) had its greatest success of the year — the launch of its first geosynchronous imaging satellite (EOS-05) on a temperamental GSLV — its employee organisations demanded clarity on its long-term plans. But this grievance was long in the making. Since the Indian Space Policy of April 2023 , the message has been clear that ISRO would, one day in the unspecified future, stop making commercial satellites and launch rockets. Clearly inspired by NASA, it expects to focus on ambitious exploratory missions and, literally, moonshots. Why would a space agency ramping up space missions upset a section of employees? This is not the paradox it presents. The letter, co-signed by nine employee associations , and addressed to the chairman, seeks clarity on staff-strength, recruitment and the outsourcing of core functions. ISRO says that it will “not be privatised or reduced”; IN-SPACe, set up to facilitate private participation, says the agency will “not be diminished”, only that the industry’s role must grow. Both are silent on the core concern — potential job losses. This brings up an underlying tension that ISRO must deal with: does its vision of India’s space sector align with its founding principles, of not being enamoured of space races and being laser-focused on space technology as a tool for social development? Or is the image of power, where India is one of a handful of space-faring countries with a mushrooming of ‘space startups’, now the bedrock of that vision?

With a budget 16 times the Department of Space’s — $24.4 billion against ₹13,705 crore — NASA too has scaled back since the 1960s: from 0.7% of American GDP in 1966 to 0.1% now, and from 36,000 civil servants at Apollo’s peak to about 14,000 today. Unlike NASA, which in its early years designed and made every nut and bolt, ISRO has always had a manufacturing relationship with the private sector (Walchandnagar, L&T). What is different is that the buzz is not about established companies building on experience but new entrants with fleeting foreign capital, most interested in satellite data as a service. No sector can hope to be static; survival can mean significant changes to how it operates. There is yet no serious reckoning with the might of China’s space programme. If India’s space sector in 2035 is to be known as a source of export earnings, a nucleus of value-added services that brings in jobs and absorbs skilled labour, then hard choices taken today may be worth it. But jumping onto a bandwagon of space — as fuel for the science fiction fantasy of billionaires and colonial notions of conquest, to align with some misplaced notion of an ‘exclusive’ club — is foolhardy. ISRO must have a transparent policy that spells this out.

editorials.title: Natural partners: On India-Belgium ties
editorials.passage:
In terms of size and engagement, Belgium is not one of India’s most important partners. However, the visit of the Belgian Prime Minister to Delhi is part of a larger puzzle of India’s ties with European countries. These have now gained salience with focus areas for India: in economic relations, defence relations and strategic ties. At the top of the agenda in talks between Prime Ministers Bart De Wever and Narendra Modi was bilateral trade opportunities once the India-European Union Free Trade Agreement (FTA) is signed — which is expected in December. India-Belgium trade is about $13 billion, a third of which is from over a century of collaboration in the diamond industry. Antwerp is a global hub for diamond trading, while Mumbai and Surat provide the biggest cutting and polishing services. However, once the EU FTA is signed, they hope to benefit from collaboration in other areas including renewable energy and food processing; the Prime Ministers agreed to set a target of doubling bilateral trade in the next five years. Despite being surrounded by friendly European allies, Belgium has a robust high-tech defence industry — small arms, drone and counter-drone technology, ammunition and naval defence — and is keen to make inroads in the Indian market, with India seeking to diversify its procurement beyond global powers. The two sides agreed on an MoU for co-development of military hardware, and signed a letter of intent on defence cooperation. India will appoint a resident defence attaché to Brussels, complementing Belgium’s move.

Statements by the two leaders, however, indicated that the visit went beyond the bilateral to a more geopolitical framing of strategic ties, both bilateral as well as between India and Europe. At a business event, Mr. De Wever said that Europe is now realising the truth of India’s “warnings” on strategic autonomy from global powers and over dependence in trade and industrial production, in particular referring to China. After the talks, Mr. Modi said that democratic values, a market economy, and people-to-people ties make India and Belgium “natural partners”, a theme he has promoted this past year, as he has stepped up visits to Europe and received a number of European leaders in Delhi, in the run-up to his Brussels visit later this year for the FTA. It is also significant that Mr. De Wever’s visit comes in the same week that New Delhi is preparing to welcome Russian President Vladimir Putin for the BRICS summit in Delhi. The engagement with Belgium demonstrates a new maturity for both European countries and India. This shows sensitivity to their respective positions on the Russia-Ukraine conflict, indicating that ties outweigh Europe’s enmity and India’s deep friendship with Moscow.

editorials.title: New map reflects resistance against expansionist claims
editorials.passage: World maps can be seen as instruments through which dominant powers exercise their influence. That is why the United Nations’ decision last week to adopt the Equal Earth projection is a significant move, reflecting a global history stretching back more than four centuries—and right up to the present moment.  This tumultuous history owes as much to Flemish geographer Gerardus Mercator’s way of projecting a round world in two dimensions as it does to high-stakes espionage carried out in Goa.In the era in which European navigators adopted Mercator’s idea—the projection the UN vote has now retired—sailing maps were keys to trading treasures. Portuguese merchants, who enjoyed a near-monopoly over Asia’s spice trade with Europe in the 16th century, closely guarded their maps, which helped them navigate the Indian Ocean. It was only when Dutch merchant Jan Huyghen van Linschoten, who served as private secretary to the Archbishop of Goa in the 1580s, surreptitiously copied these maps and published them in Europe in the 1590s that the colonial era was effectively flung open. The information, coupled with Mercator’s projection published a few decades earlier, made sailing easier for transcontinental merchants.The biggest consequence of last week’s change is that equatorial nations, which appeared much smaller on the Mercator projection, will be represented more equitably. Consider the oddity of having seen Africa as barely bigger than Greenland on maps, though the continent can fit 14 Greenlands within it, with room to spare. As the foreign minister of Togo, the nation that proposed the UN resolution, explained: “There is scientific proof, so we all have to accept the reality.”.India, one of the 164 nations backing the resolution, later clarified that no new map can deny India’s sovereign claim over lands in Jammu and Kashmir. The vote and the clarification underline the political implications of modern cartography. Like most African nations, India is acutely aware of the danger that unratified maps pose in legitimising expansionist claims. It reminds us that disagreements with China over the lines drawn in Ladakh, Sikkim and Arunachal Pradesh cannot be allowed to morph into alternative realities about sovereignty over those regions.It was telling that the US was the only nation to oppose the UN resolution. The stance reflected Donald Trump’s worldview, in which all it apparently takes to rechristen the Gulf of Mexico, Lake Ontario and even the US state of New Mexico is a broad-nibbed pen. Even in the era of Google Maps, such transgressions cannot be allowed to stand..Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

editorials.title: Constant vigil needs to enforce building rules
editorials.passage: How long can Delhi continue to treat building and fire safety matters to be addressed post mortem? The collapse of a student accommodation in Satya Niketan on Sunday, where renovation and basement work was reportedly underway, is another reminder of how poorly regulation works in the national capital. It has now emerged that the building did not have construction sanctions and a fire safety certificate. As a result, seven lives have been lost, while five others were injured. The first question is why such a building was allowed to operate. The Delhi High Court correctly expressed concern about the regulatory practices of the Municipal Corporation of Delhi.This is not the first such case. In May, six people died when an unauthorised building collapsed in Saidulajab. An inquiry found that the MCD knew about illegal construction, failed to act on complaints and fabricated inspection records. In June, 23 people died in a fire at a Malviya Nagar bed-and-breakfast that was authorised for six rooms, but was running 26 rooms without a fire licence. The Mundka fire in 2022 killed 27 people. The Karol Bagh hotel fire in 2019 killed 17 people.There have been committees, inquiries and recommendations after these incidents. In June, the Supreme Court’s amicus curiae asked for directions to municipal authorities to conduct structural audits and seal or demolish illegal structures. After the Malviya Nagar fire, the government announced committees to survey and seal unsafe buildings. Delhi’s disaster management plans also called for identifying vulnerable buildings and enforcing construction regulations..So why does the system keep failing citizens? Delhi’s new Master Plan for the next 20 years again proposes measures to prevent hazardous, unplanned and non-compliant structures—similar to the rules issued in 2007 that have evidently not been strictly enforced. What guarantees that this time it will be different?What Delhi needs is a system to check building approvals, fire clearances, structural safety certificates and violations. Buildings found unsafe should not continue to operate while files move between departments. Responsibility must be fixed for inspections, approvals and failures to act. With governance going digital, lack of access to updated information on building approvals, violations and inspections can no longer be an excuse. A city cannot call a building disaster an accident when the risks were visible, documented and repeatedly warned about. The credibility of regulation itself is at stake..Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

editorials.title: Quick Take | A Latin lesson
editorials.passage: While India struggles to implement women’s reservation in one-third of seats at the Centre and in states, it should look closer at the countries where women account for more than half the elected national legislatures. The case of Rwanda, where women occupy almost two-thirds of the seats, is an outlier because its 1994 genocide slashed the country’s male population. But higher representation in four other countries listed by University of Gothenburg’s V Dem Institute— Cuba, Nicaragua, Bolivia and Mexico—is testament to persistent lawmaking on gender balance. One of the biggest lessons from Latin America—which in some ways is no less patriarchal than India—is that high levels of women’s education can go a long way in enacting more equitable laws..Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

editorials.title: Crisis of the commons: Clean air for climate action begins with accountability
Mountain without a border ~ I
editorials.passage:
Somewhere above the line where Nepal ends and Tibet begins, in the last week of August, a mass of ice and the rock it had gripped for centuries let go at once. No sentry recorded the moment, and no border guard could have. It began as a single event and, within minutes, became many ~ a surge down the throat of a valley, a river briefly dammed by its own wreckage and then bursting through the dam it had built, a grey wall of water arriving at settlements that had heard only a far-off crack and, after it, a sound like a train where there was no railway. 

By the time the noise reached the towns below, the thing that made it was already among them. What came down was not one disaster but a chain, each link handing its force to the next. The failure high on the mountain fed the river; the swollen river tore at the valley floor; the valley floor surrendered its bridges, its road cuttings, its penstocks and powerhouses. At least six major hydroelectric plants ~ the patient work of decades, the machinery meant to turn this ferocious water into light and revenue ~ were broken. On the Tibetan side the trade hub at Gyirong, the busy doorway through which goods and pilgrims pass between Nepal and China, was battered into silence. 

Lorries that had crossed at dawn did not return by dusk, or at all. Then, when the water fell back, came the arithmetic of the missing, and it is here that the disaster shows its true shape. Close to 3,000 people are still unaccounted for. They are Nepali villagers and Tibetan traders; they are also, by the reckoning of India’s own Ministry of External Affairs, 275 Indian nationals ~ pilgrims and migrant workers who had climbed into these mountains for reasons of faith or wages and are now entries on a list. 

One flood; three national ledgers. The water kept no such books on its way down. India did what a decent neighbour does, and did it quickly. Relief flew north within days; engineers and bridging teams went with it, because when every span is gone the first gift worth giving is a way back across. There is nothing to fault in that response except its shape, which is the shape of every response we know how to mount ~ a convoy dispatched, a photograph taken, a mission stood down when the road reopens. We are very good at the convoy. We have never built the thing that would make the convoy unnecessary. 

Consider what Nepal now faces alone. A reconstruction bill its own officials already reckon in the region of four to five billion dollars is not a sum a small mountain economy raises between monsoons. Much of what must be rebuilt is not Nepali in any useful sense: the hydropower that failed was selling, or hoped to sell, current across the border; the trade route that closed carried other countries’ goods; the tourists who will not come this winter were the incomes of guides and lodge-keepers who never filed a customs form in their lives. The ledger is national. The loss is not. And here the disaster stops being a foreign bulletin and becomes a mirror. The same geology that gave way above Gyirong runs unbroken through our own high country ~ the dam-crowded valleys of Himachal Pradesh, the young and shaken slopes of Sikkim, the gorges of Jammu and Kashmir where run-of-river schemes are stacked one above another like rungs on a ladder. 

We laid those roads and powerhouses along the valley floors because that is the flattest ground the mountains offer, which is also, precisely, the lane the water takes when it comes down. Sikkim showed us as much only two years ago, when the South Lhonak lake burst its wall of moraine above the Teesta and carried off a flagship dam in a single night. The failure in Nepal and Tibet was not an omen sent for our instruction; it was an earlier instance of a story whose later chapters have our names in them. 

To read it as somebody else's misfortune is to misread it entirely. The reason we keep misreading it is that our whole apparatus for disaster rests on an assumption the mountains quietly violate. That apparatus was built for the plains ~ for the cyclone that makes landfall on one coast, the flood that fills one basin, the earthquake whose damage, however vast, falls within a single set of borders and answers to a single chain of command. The Himalaya honours no such tidiness. It is one hydrological system wearing several flags, a single tilted watershed in which a lake that bursts beneath a glacier on one side drowns a town on another and dims a grid a frontier away. 

Worse, the knowledge that might see the danger coming is divided by the very same borders as the danger: much of the ice and rock that menaces a Nepali valley gathers on a plateau another state monitors, and the satellites and expertise that could read it in time sit across a line the debris will cross in minutes. Sovereignty over territory has never meant sovereignty over the water, ice and rock that move through it. This is not a charge that anyone behaved badly. Nepal grieved and counted; India flew its missions and brought its people home; China, this time, was not a bystander to a Himalayan catastrophe but the owner of some of its heaviest losses, and that symmetry is new. 

Each did competently what its own map told it to do. The failure is not of effort or of goodwill but of design ~ of asking three national systems, each blind beyond its own boundary, to meet a single event that respects none of them. Lists of the missing pass between three governments in three scripts and three protocols; a forecast one of them makes and does not share is a diary entry, not a warning. What the water demonstrated, in short, is that the border is real to us and imaginary to the mountain. The Himalaya was never a wall. 

It was a watershed that happened to be high, and empires drew their lines across it because lines are what empires know how to draw; the ice did not countersign them. We can go on pretending otherwise, dispatching convoys after each catastrophe and standing them down when the photographs are filed. 

Or we can ask the harder question the flood has set us ~ not how to grieve better or give more, but how three neighbours who do not trust one another might nonetheless agree to watch the same ice, sound the same alarm and keep the same roads open before the next mass of it lets go. That question, and the uncomfortable architecture it demands, is the subject of the second part.  

(The writer is a practising Chartered Accountant. He can be reached at kannan@cakt.in)

editorials.title: IWT remains in abeyance
editorials.passage:
The preamble of the Indus Water Treaty (IWT), signed on 19 September 1960 between India and Pakistan mentions that it is being done in a “spirit of goodwill and friendship”. It was expected that the two sides would maintain that spirit and be good neighbours. India under the agreement contributed financially to enable Pakistan to construct canals and other waterways to offset the impact of the treaty and shift its dependency from eastern rivers to western ones. 

The sub-continent has undergone vast changes over the years, necessitating a re-evaluation of the treaty. India has been requesting Pakistan to re-negotiate the treaty since 2023 due to changing dynamics. The reasons include enhanced water demands for agriculture, drinking and industry due to increased population, impact of climate change, advances in hydropower technology and interpretation of the treaty’s dispute resolution process. This was never accepted by Pakistan, basically because the treaty favoured them. Operation Gibraltar launched by Pakistan in 1965 was the first instance of breaking the clause of “goodwill and friendship” under which the treaty was negotiated. 

India still adhered to its terms. It stuck to the agreement despite 1971, Kargil and support to terrorism in J and K. India did so because it believed that the people of Pakistan must not suffer because of misdeeds of its military leadership, which always sought to inflict injury on India, either through wars of supporting terrorism. There is always a limit to patience within a country. Finally, running out of patience on Pakistan backing terrorism and offsetting basic conditions of goodwill and friendship with Pahalgam, India decided to hold the treaty in ‘abeyance.’ Holding the treaty in ‘abeyance’ is considered by legal experts to indicate ‘political intent’, as the term is unrecognized in international treaty law. 

In response, rather than stopping support to terrorism, Pakistan’s military and political leadership threatened India with conflict, approached the Permanent Court of Arbitration (PCA) in The Hague and attempted to internationalize the issue by conducting international seminars, publishing its viewpoints in global media networks exploiting its embedded journalists, and by playing the victim card. Pakistan’s defence minister, Khawaja Asif went on to state, “The moment we feel that our national security – and water is part of our national security – is threatened, we will go to war against India. 

Definitely.” Their PM, Shehbaz Sharief, stated at the SCO meeting in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, “Water is the lifeblood of our region. It sustains millions of lives, nourishes our land and secures the very future of our coming generations.” He had earlier mentioned in Islamabad, “I declare in clear terms that every single drop of Pakistan's water is our red line. If India does not come to its senses, it will be responded to directly.” Asim Munir, busy running around the globe attempting to negotiate conflicts, in one of his rare visits to Pakistan and even rarer meeting with his generals, stated that the Pakistani military would “undertake all measures necessary to ensure availability of Pakistan’s rightful share of water as per directives of the government and aspirations of the people of Pakistan.” 

However, he is aware of limitations of his armed forces, and the fact that India’s retaliation would be brutal. Pakistan conducted an international conference on IWT in end June in Islamabad titled “Indus Waters Treaty as an Enduring Legal and Institutional Framework.” It brought in dubious experts on the treaty. Pakistan’s leaders began stating that they are the true custodians of the Indus heritage, including its water. For eight decades, Pakistan, which considered Muhammad Bin Qasim as its first citizen, suddenly realized the importance of the Indus Valley civilization. 

Despite all its drama, its claims fell flat. Playing the victim card, Pakistan approached the UN Security Council, of which it is a rotating member. Nothing moved. Not one member joined in criticizing India. Its foreign minister, Ishaq Dar, broached the subject when his UK and Canadian counterparts visited Islamabad, but as usual, the result was zero. Possibly Pakistan has a visitor once a month and it raises the IWT with each one, while India has a stream of visitors and not a single one has even broached the topic. Pakistan attempted to bring in the World Bank, which had negotiated the treaty. World Bank head Ajay Singh Banga mentioned that the bank has no role in bilateral issues. 

So much for Pakistan’s diplomatic efforts. In end August, the Pakistan embassy in Washington hosted a discussion on “The Indus Waters Treaty: South Asian Security at Crossroads,” hoping to impress policy makers in the US into applying pressure on India. It was another in its list of failures. It failed to draw in any international expert. The only US academician who attended was a professor from Boston University, who had earlier been VC of Lahore University. To highlight the Indian viewpoint and challenge Pakistan’s game on the IWT, the Indian ambassador to Washington, Vinay Kwatra, wrote in The Week, “Pakistan spent half a century dismantling that goodwill and friendship. 

The abeyance merely acknowledges what Pakistan's conduct had already destroyed.” Pakistan’s ambassador responded in an article in the same magazine, discussing technical aspects of the treaty, bypassing India’s claim of “dismantling goodwill and friendship.” Islamabad approached the PCA in The Hague. India refused to participate. It was a one-sided representation. India rejected the court’s ruling mentioning, “This so-called Court of Arbitration has no jurisdiction whatsoever to pronounce on India’s sovereign decisions,” adding, “its pronouncements, now or in the future, will have no effect on India’s actions in connection with the projects being undertaken by India.” 

Since India decided to stay away from PCA hearings, it was Pakistan which was forced to pay for expenditure on both sides. This has been estimated to be USD 600,000 (300,000 per nation). It would have been cheaper for Pakistan to come to the negotiating table and discuss fresh terms and conditions, including stopping support to terrorism. It spent money and achieved nothing at the end of the day. Pakistan has played every card up its sleeve, diplomatic, military and legal amongst others. Each card has failed. It has just one choice left. Adhere to India’s core demand of stopping terrorism and then re-negotiate the treaty. Unless it does so, it would continue crying with no avail, while the treaty will remain in abeyance. 

(The writer is a retired Major-General of the Indian Army)

editorials.title: A flood isn’t just a natural disaster
editorials.passage:
A river does not know the language of development. A mountain does not understand a building permit. A glacier recognises no political boundary, yet human beings increasingly behave as though nature must adjust itself to our plans. The devastation in Nepal should make us ask a more uncomfortable question than simply, “Why did it rain so heavily?” or “Why did the glacier collapse?” An extreme natural event may trigger a disaster, but human decisions often determine its scale. 

When settlements, roads, bridges and economic assets are placed in vulnerable locations while natural protection is destroyed, a hazard becomes a catastrophe. We have become good at predicting hazards but poor at respecting warnings. We are engineering the landscape to make civilisation possible while simultaneously engineering away its capacity to protect civilisation. This is not merely an engineering failure. It is a failure of responsibility - a willingness to ignore nature in the name of progress. Modern development asks, “What can we build here?” It should first ask, “What can this landscape safely carry?” Climate change makes this question more urgent. 

Burning coal, oil and gas, deforestation and destruction of natural ecosystems increase greenhouse gases and warm the planet. In the Himalayas, warming is affecting glaciers, snow and rainfall, increasing the risks of floods and landslides. But climate change should not become an excuse for poor decisions. A forest is not merely a collection of trees. It is a living community of trees, shrubs, grasses, insects, birds, fungi and microorganisms that protects the land and regulates water. Roots hold soil, vegetation slows rainfall, organic matter stores water, and biodiversity helps forests recover from disturbances. 

Destroying forests or their biodiversity means losing a natural system that slows floods, prevents erosion, stabilises slopes and releases water gradually. A forest may still look green after losing much of its biodiversity, but it may no longer provide the protection of a healthy ecosystem. Then comes the assault on the river. We encroach upon floodplains and later describ e the river as “encroaching” upon us. We narrow channels, occupy banks, fill wetlands and cover soil with concrete, then wonder why water refuses to obey the drainage plan. Unregulated mining of sand, stone and gravel can destabilise riverbeds and accelerate erosion. 

Hill cutting without proper geological assessment can turn stable slopes into landslide hazards. Development is necessary, but excess can be dangerous. A road providing essential connectivity is development; a road cut through an unstable mountain for speculative construction is something else. Infrastructure driven by speed, prestige or profit, without regard to ecological limits, becomes a gamble with public safety. Development that destroys the natural systems on which society depends is not genuine progress. It is borrowed prosperity, with nature eventually presenting the bill. Corruption is not merely money changing hands. 

There is also corruption of judgment: scientific warnings ignored because they are inconvenient; environmental assessments reduced to paperwork; safety margins compromised; political visibility valued above ecological necessity; and responsibilities divided among agencies until nobody is accountable. Scientists may produce excellent data, engineers sound designs and meteorologists timely warnings. But if scientific knowledge does not change construction, land-use or evacuation decisions, science becomes decoration. We often ask scientists to explain disasters after they occur instead of asking why known risks were allowed to accumulate. Education must therefore change. 

Children should learn not only that floods follow heavy rain, but to ask: Where did the water come from? Where did the forest go? Why was the settlement built there? Where is the floodplain? Why was the river narrowed? Was a warning issued, and who acted on it? Such education teaches children to understand the relationship between human decisions and nature rather than simply memorising environmental facts. We speak of conquering mountains, controlling rivers and harnessing nature. But a mountain does not surrender because a road is cut into it, and a river does not become obedient because concrete walls surround it. Nature has limits. When we cross them, nature reminds us who is really in control. 

The Nepal tragedy should not end with rescue, compensation and reconstruction. Rebuilding the same roads and settlements in the same hazardous places may simply prepare the next disaster. Hazard maps must guide land-use plans; watershed planning must precede isolated projects; ecological limits must be assessed before construction; environmental assessments must be genuinely independent; warnings must reach communities; and some high-risk areas may have to remain free of permanent settlement. 

Scientists must speak beyond their laboratories. Engineers must sometimes say “no”. Bureaucrats must reject unsafe projects. Political leaders must understand that preventing a disaster earns no ribbon-cutting ceremony - but may save thousands of lives. Citizens must also recognise that environmental protection is not an obstacle to development; it is the insurance that makes development durable. The most frightening lesson from Nepal is not simply that the Himalayas are becoming more dangerous. It is that we are becoming increasingly dangerous to ourselves because we have forgotten how to live within the limits of the landscape. 

(The writer is former Senior Scientist, Central Pollution Control Board)

editorials.title: Unsafe Profits
editorials.passage:
The collapse of building housing students in Delhi’s Satya Niketan should not be treated as another entry in India’s long catalogue of urban accidents. The immediate priority is to rescue those trapped and establish the precise cause. But the circumstances already raise a larger and more uncomfortable question: how does an ageing building, showing signs of structural distress, continue to house dozens of young people? Satya Niketan is not an anonymous residential neighbourhood. 

Its proximity to Delhi University’s South Campus has turned it into a dense marketplace for student housing. Private paying guest accommodations have proliferated to meet a genuine demand, creating a lucrative economy around young people who arrive in the capital needing somewhere affordable to live. Yet this commercial success has created an obvious regulatory challenge: who ensures that buildings adapted and intensified for student accommodation remain structurally safe? The collapsed building reportedly housed a 75-bed private PG. Accounts suggest that it had previously been rented as flats before being handed over to a commercial accommodation operator. 

There were also reports of repair or construction work at the lower levels and claims that the structure had shown signs of tilting. These claims require proper investigation. But they make the eventual inquiry about far more than a single engineering failure. What is rarely addressed is the system that allows structurally questionable buildings to remain occupied until disaster provides the inspection that should have happened earlier. Student housing deserves particular scrutiny. 

Students are vulnerable consumers in the urban property market. Living away from their families, they have neither the expertise nor bargaining power to assess whether a building has been illegally modified, inadequately maintained or dangerously overloaded. Parents, meanwhile, assume that a prominently advertised and commercially operated hostel has passed some basic threshold of safety. That assumption may be dangerously misplaced. Delhi's municipal authorities cannot plausibly plead ignorance of the transformation of neighbourhoods such as Satya Niketan, or of countless others especially in Delhi’s villages where the municipal writ runs weak. 

The conversion of residential properties into high-density student accommodation is visible, commercially organised and sustained by predictable demand. The investigation must therefore extend beyond identifying the immediate trigger of the collapse. Were structural alterations authorised? Did the building’s use change without appropriate safety certification? Who approved ongoing work? Were complaints or warning signs recorded? And crucially, what responsibility rests with those who profited from packing large numbers of students into an ageing structure? 

A city cannot outsource the safety of its young residents to landlords and market forces. Private accommodation may be a business, but housing students carries responsibilities that cannot end with collecting rent. The Satya Niketan collapse exposes a wider pattern of weak oversight in Delhi’s booming student housing economy. Simply prosecuting a few individuals after the fact will not be enough, heads of municipal and police authorities must also roll. The real test will be whether authorities inspect the buildings still standing ~ before another pile of rubble forces them to.

editorials.title: Bibi’s shadow
editorials.passage:
Benjamin Netanyahu’s most consequential electoral victory may not require him to win Israel’s forthcoming parliamentary election. That paradox lies at the heart of the campaign now taking shape. Polls may show former military chief Gadi Eisenkot emerging as a serious challenger, but Israel’s fragmented political system means that defeating Netanyahu at the ballot box is only the first hurdle. 

The harder question is whether an alternative government can be assembled without accepting the political boundaries Netanyahu has spent years constructing. Israel's electoral system makes coalitionbuilding unavoidable. No party can realistically govern alone in the 120-member Knesset; a majority requires 61 seats. For the opposition, this arithmetic may eventually require some form of cooperation with Arab parties. Netanyahu has seized on that possibility, portraying such alliances as inherently illegitimate and casting his opponents as dependent on forces hostile to Israel’s interests. 

The tactic is politically effective precisely because it exploits one of Israeli democracy’s unresolved contradictions. Arab citizens account for roughly a fifth of the population and possess full voting rights, yet their elected representatives have long been treated by much of the political establishment as unsuitable partners in national government. That convention was briefly challenged in 2021, when Mansour Abbas’s Ra’am party joined Naftali Bennett's governing coalition. 

The experiment demonstrated that Arab participation in government was constitutionally possible and politically manageable. Yet it did not fundamentally alter the deeper suspicion surrounding Arab parties. The coming election may determine whether that experiment was an exception or the beginning of a genuine transformation. Eisenkot’s predicament illustrates Netanyahu’s broader strategy. A challenger seeking to unite Israel’s disparate anti-Netanyahu forces needs ideological flexibility. But every possible compromise can be weaponised. The wider the coalition, the easier it becomes to portray it as incoherent, weak or dependent upon unacceptable partners. 

This is more than conventional negative campaigning. It is an attempt to determine the limits of legitimate politics before the election has even been held. Netanyahu understands that political power does not reside solely in office. Leaders also exercise power by defining what their opponents are permitted to say, whom they can work with and which compromises carry an electoral penalty. If Eisenkot is forced continually to demonstrate nationalist credentials, he may find his eventual room for manoeuvre shrinking even if Netanyahu loses. 

The danger for Israel extends beyond one election. Democracies become progressively narrower when elected representatives of large sections of the population are treated as permanently legitimate voters but inherently illegitimate governors. Such an arrangement creates representation without genuine participation. Netanyahu’s opponents therefore face a challenge larger than removing a long-serving prime minister. They must decide whether they merely want a different coalition or a different conception of Israeli democracy. That distinction could determine the campaign’s true winner. Netanyahu may lose the premiership yet retain something almost as valuable: the power to define the political boundaries within which his successors must govern.

editorials.title: Strategic embrace
editorials.passage:
A series of elections in the last 10 years has led to the election of right-wing leaders in Latin America. In Central America, these include Nayib Bukele in El Salvador, Nasry Asfura in Honduras, Laura Fernández Delgado in Costa Rica, and José Raúl Mulino in Panama. In the Amazonia region of South America, they include Abelardo de la Espriella in Colombia and Daniel Noboa in Ecuador. In the continent’s Andean region, Peru elected Keiko Fujimori, the daughter of the country’s former president and dictator, Alberto Fujimori, as president, while Bolivia elected Rodrigo Paz. The southern cone has witnessed the election of Santiago Peña in Paraguay and Javier Milei in Argentina as their presidents, respectively. The Donald Trump administration is backing these right-wing leaders to combat narco-trafficking and roll back China’s economic and security footprint in the region.

In terms of economic policies, these presidents promise a vision of free market and limited government with local flavours. These include President Bukele making Bitcoin a currency for El Salvador or the thwarted attempt by President Milei to use the US dollar as the Argentinian currency. These presidents have also promised the restoration of law and order, which has been threatened by criminal gangs, many aligned with narco-trafficking cartels, and by corrupt and slow criminal justice systems. Their foreign policy seeks alignment with the United States of America.

Whereas the Joe Biden administration distanced itself from right-wing leaders like Bukele and Brazil’s Jair Bolsonaro, Trump has embraced all of them. The explicit focus of the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, on realigning Latin America — in terms of diplomacy, security, and trade — with the US has also led to the extradition of Venezuela’s left-wing dictator, Nicolás Maduro, in January 2026 and an increase in economic and political pressure on Cuba’s dictator, Miguel Díaz-Canel. The only left-wing dictatorship that has not felt US pressure yet is that of Daniel Ortega in Nicaragua.

In terms of security, the US sees China’s combination of economic and security influence as a major threat in Latin America. Consequently, the Trump administration leveraged the US’s position as the canal’s largest user — 40% of the total traffic and, therefore, revenue generator — to pressure Panama to oust Hong Kong-based CK Hutchison from controlling two terminals at the canal’s Atlantic and Pacific ends. The US also arranged for the sale of used F-16 fighter aircraft from Denmark to Argentina to pre-empt the procurement of new Chinese JF-17 fighter jets. As an aside, India’s Tejas LCA lost the bid.

Other key decisions based on a combination of economic and security interests included the Trump government continuing the Biden-era support for tiny, oil-rich Guyana in deterring its larger and better-armed neighbour, Venezuela, from annexing the Essequibo region. Trump also tried but failed to reopen a naval base in Manta, Ecuador, after a 2025 referendum could not reverse the outcome of the one in 2009 which, propelled by the left-wing former president, Rafael Correa, shut all foreign bases. The setback, however, has not stopped a rise in defence and security cooperation centred on preventing narco-trafficking.

In terms of trade, though, the Trump regime’s desire to impose tariffs on imports of goods threatens to undercut trade with the region. Despite the US Supreme Court’s abrogation of Trump’s tariffs, the partial roll back by the Trump dispensation’s imposition of a 10% and, then, 15% global tariff continues to burden trade ties because it ignores the fact that the US enjoys sizeable trade surpluses with certain countries and deficits with others.

The tariffs should really be seen as an attempt to reset US ties with the region from one based on free trade and multilateral organisations like the Dominican Republic-Central America Free Trade Agreement or the Caribbean Community and Common Market to one centred on preferential access to the US market and direct investments based on alignment with American policy objectives. These include controlling drug cartels and reducing China’s economic and security footprint in the region. There are also other such conditions as avoiding unfair labour practices and environmental damage, long sought for by US labour organisations. Tariffs on particular goods can therefore be reduced or increased contingent upon a country’s performance on these yardsticks.

On the one hand, regional exports critical to US manufacturing, like copper products from Peru and Chile or lithium and aluminium from Argentina, have been exempted from US tariffs. Mexico also retained preferential access via the North American Free Trade Agreement’s new avatar, the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement. The announcements by the US seeking preferential trade agreements and increased US investments for Colombia have been used to lend support to the recently elected president, Espriella. A special US credit line was also assured to Argentina that shored up domestic support for President Milei which may have contributed to his party’s victory in the October 2025 legislative elections. On the other hand, the Trump administration is also allegedly moving to exclude Nicaragua from the CAFTA-DR to put pressure on President Ortega, thereby also rewarding El Salvador and Guatemala by forcing manufacturers in Nicaragua to relocate to these countries.

These US efforts, however, remain threatened by domestic political dynamics that the Trump government cannot fully control. Some regional leaders were elected by narrow margins. For example, Peru’s Keiko Fujimori won against her opponent by 50,000 votes out of 18 million. Colombia’s Espriella won by 251,000 votes: 1% more than his opponent. Broad presidential coalitions centred on personalities also lack majorities in the legislature which threatens gridlocks. Chile’s José Antonio Kast won by a convincing 58.16% over his opponent, but his party controls only 31 out of the 155 seats in the Chamber of Deputies and 5 among 50 seats in the Senate. In Honduras’s National Congress, a unicameral legislature, the 124-year-old Asfura’s National Party controls only 49 out of 128 seats.

The risk of unpredictable slides into authoritarianism remains. El Salvador’s incumbent party, Nueva Ideas, controls 54 out of 60 seats in the unicameral legislative assembly, but Bukele pushed to remove term limits on presidential elections in 2025: a pathway to remain in power indefinitely.

In this — the risk of authoritarianism — these South American nations may be mirroring the US.

Vasabjit Banerjee is an Associate Professor of Political Science at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville and a Non-Resident Fellow at the Observer Research Foundation, America

editorials.title: Metaphorical fire
editorials.passage:
When The Metamorphosis appeared in 1915, it did not arrive bearing a manifesto. It brought a travelling salesman who woke one morning to discover that he had become something unspeakable. Kafka called him “ ungeheures Ungeziefer ”, a monstrous vermin. He refused to identify the creature. He even instructed his publisher that the insect should never be drawn. Readers, being readers, ignored him and took matters into their own hands.

Illustrators gave Gregor Samsa legs, antennae and a shell. Translators reached for the nearest common man’s horror, the cockroach. Popular culture transformed literature’s most ambiguous insect into its most recognisable one. In South Korea, scholars have documented how the cockroach became a recurring metaphor in internet culture, satire and political ridicule. The insect ceased to belong to Kafka and entered public vocabulary as shorthand for dehumanisation, social disgust and the bureaucratic violence of reducing human beings into pests.

And now, the cockroach has crawled off the page and entered our screens, newspapers and real life. Suddenly, ‘cockroaches’ are everywhere, in every disillusioned youth, in every disappointed citizen. Those born in the later decades of the twentieth century have chosen this symbol to be their personal signature, demanding to be recognised and legitimised.

This is how literature works. It rarely starts movements by issuing instructions. It furnishes them with metaphors.

George Orwell’s Nineteen Eighty-Four may be the greatest political lexicon ever to be disguised as fiction. Every debate over facial recognition, data surveillance and State overreach still reaches instinctively for Orwell’s work. The phrases, “Big Brother”, “Thought Police”, “Doublethink” and “Room 101”, have become so deeply embedded in the public lexicon that they often survive independently of the novel. Orwell did not merely imagine a dictatorship. He permanently altered the language through which democracies describe their fears.

Joseph Heller achieved something equally remarkable — almost by accident.

Catch-22 began as military satire, exposing the absurdity of war through bureaucratic logic that fed endlessly upon itself. Today, the title has become a talismanic resolution for every impossible administrative puzzle. You need experience to get a job. You need a job to gain experience. Bureaucracy, it turns out, required only two words to expose its greatest absurdity. Does this bring a smile to Heller’s face in some realm?

Sometimes, literature changes not language but law.

Harriet Beecher Stowe’s Uncle Tom’s Cabin did not abolish slavery by itself, but it transformed an economic debate into a moral emergency. Millions who had encountered slavery as statistics suddenly met it as human suffering. Whether or not Abraham Lincoln ever called Stowe “the little lady who started this great war” matters less than why the quote survived. It recognised a truth politicians have always known but rarely admitted: stories often persuade where speeches fail.

Upton Sinclair learnt the same lesson, albeit with considerable disappointment.

He wrote The Jungle intending to expose the brutal exploitation of immigrant workers in Chicago’s meatpacking industry. Readers were instead horrified by what might be lurking inside their sausages. Public outrage helped usher in sweeping food safety reforms, including the Pure Food and Drug Act and the Federal Meat Inspection Act, in the United States of America. Sinclair later sighed that he had “aimed at the public’s heart and by accident hit it in the stomach”.

Even fiction that celebrates radical individualism has found an organised afterlife.

Ayn Rand’s Atlas Shrugged evolved from a sprawling philosophical novel into a foundational text for libertarian and free-market politics in America. The protagonist, John Galt, transcended fiction to become an ideological mascot. Few novels have supplied an entire political movement with so durable a mythology.

And how can we leave out Margaret Atwood?

Few authors can claim to have designed a uniform for global protest: the scarlet robes and the white bonnets of The Handmaid’s Tale now appear outside legislatures from Washington to Buenos Aires, Dublin to Delhi. Protesters opposing restrictions on reproductive rights rarely need banners explaining themselves. They simply arrive dressed as Atwood’s handmaids.

Literature manufactures metaphors robust enough to survive their creators. Kafka never wrote the word, ‘cockroach’; Orwell did not coin the term, ‘surveillance capitalism’; Heller never imagined university admission portals; Atwood did not design protest merchandise. That is perhaps the most unsettling lesson of all. Once a book enters public consciousness, it no longer belongs to its author. It belongs to history’s imagination.

There are revolutions that begin with barricades. And then there are those that begin with a sentence.

Monjorika Bose writes on politics, public affairs, urban transformation and culture

editorials.title: River renaissance
editorials.passage:
In 1884, Jyotirindranath Tagore did something remarkably modern. He launched a commercial steamer service between Khulna and Barisal, reviving a vision his grandfather, Dwarkanath Tagore, had pursued four decades earlier through the India General Steam Navigation Company.

Before highways and railways dominated transport, the Bengal delta sustained one of Asia's most integrated inland transport systems. Jute from Narayanganj, Barisal and Faridpur floated to the mills of Calcutta. Coal from Raniganj travelled upstream. Steamers connected Khulna, Goalundo, Chandpur, Dhubri and the Brahmaputra river system in a network that helped make the port of Calcutta the second busiest in the British empire.

The Partition fractured that natural economy. The 1965 Indo-Pakistan War completed the rupture by suspending inland navigation. Assam and the Northeast lost their shortest access to the sea, while Calcutta forfeited its riverine hinterland. What disappeared was not merely a transport network but an economic ecosystem in which rivers served simultaneously as trade corridors, labour markets, sites of cultural exchanges and ecological assets.

The Protocol on Inland Water Transit and Trade, signed after Bangladesh's liberation, sought to recover part of that lost connectivity. Over successive renewals, it expanded to 10 protocol routes, new terminals at Dhubri and Pangaon, access through the Rupnarayan via Kolaghat, and the proposed Jogighopa multimodal hub linking the Northeast with Bhutan. Yet reality has consistently lagged behind promise.

Treaties create legal corridors; but only dredging, hydrographic surveys, navigation aids, river training works and efficient terminals can transform them into viable trade routes. Much of the network still suffers from inadequate dredging, seasonal draft restrictions, delayed terminals and cumbersome customs. The Munshiganj terminal remains unrealised, the Nakugaon-Dalu corridor has scarcely progressed, and permanent jetties on Tripura's Gomati waterway remain incomplete.

This is why 2026 assumes significance. With Bangladesh's new government under Prime Minister Tarique Rahman sending congenial signals, Delhi, Calcutta and Dhaka have an opportunity to pursue a common river agenda. Equally, China's overtures on the Teesta Barrage project underline why India cannot afford a strategic drift. West Bengal's new government enjoys political alignment with New Delhi. For the first time in decades, the three capitals have an opportunity to pursue a shared river strategy.

Political convergence, however, will achieve little unless rivers become the centrepiece of public investment. West Bengal should accelerate the Kolaghat protocol terminal, establish Geonkhali as a logistics hub, expand jetties, modernise river information systems, and integrate the Hooghly-Rupnarayan network with National Waterway-1. The Bengal budget emphasises a chain of river jetties. This is encouraging, but success depends on implementation and ease of connectivity.

Years of neglect of river morphology and the declining navigability of the Hooghly have steadily undermined Bengal's river economy. Every monsoon, farmland disappears and embankments give way. Dredging must form part of an integrated strategy of sediment management, bank stabilisation and scientifically designed river-training works.

The challenge extends beyond engineering into geopolitics. The 1996 Ganga Water Treaty expires in December 2026. India seeks greater flexibility; Bangladesh seeks assurances on lean-season flows and remains wary of the proposed Padma Barrage. Water cannot become an instrument of pressure if it is to underpin regional integration. Bengal's next chapter will not be written through expressways alone. It will also be written in dredged channels, resilient embankments and renewed waterborne trade linking India and Bangladesh.

Gautam Chakraborti was formerly Security and Heritage Advisor with SMPK

editorials.title: Be clear: Editorial on India's GDP debate and need for data transparency
editorials.passage:
India’s latest GDP estimate has had its doubters and defenders. The government has reported real GDP growth of 7.8% in the first quarter of 2026-27. This is a surprisingly encouraging figure amidst global economic headwinds. But the former finance secretary, Subhash Chandra Garg, has questioned this figure because nominal GDP for the corresponding quarter of 2025-26 was revised from about Rs 86 lakh crore under the old series to Rs 80 lakh crore under the new one. A lower starting point, Mr Garg has argued, can produce a higher growth rate. Mr Garg’s contention has not gone unchallenged. His critics state that the former finance secretary has compared figures drawn from different base years and methodologies. Rising credit, exports, investment, vehicle sales and industrial production are also being presented as evidence of robust economic activity. Experts receptive to the current GDP figure have also argued that the new system adjusts the prices of inputs and outputs separately, which can produce a low manufacturing deflator even when prices are rising elsewhere.

These claims and counterclaims have only added to public confusion. One way of clearing the air would be for the Centre to show precisely how the revised estimate was reached and why it was needed. Such a disclosure is essential because official data have, on many occasions, been brought under a cloud. The delayed Census, the withdrawal of the 2017 consumption survey, and 16 critical government datasets that were delayed for years to avoid release before the 2024 general elections are just some instances that have led to suspicion of data being cherry-picked for public consumption. The Centre must publish its complete sources and methods, the deflators used, and a sector-wise reconciliation between the old and new estimates. The resultant — enhanced — clarity would also help answer the concern raised by the former governor of the Reserve Bank of India, Raghuram Rajan: if India has sustained such strong growth, why has it failed to generate corresponding private investment, foreign direct investment and decent employment? Everyday economic conditions in the country lend Mr Rajan’s question its force. Households continue to battle inflationary pressures and dips in savings; jobs are not being created at the required scale either. GDP does not measure individual welfare, but sustained growth must eventually be reflected in improved employment, earnings and material security. When official claims of prosperity remain difficult to recognise in the lives of citizens, demands for transparency cannot be dismissed as motivated or partisan.

editorials.title: War In limbo: Editorial on the US-Iran war and the cycle of escalation
editorials.passage:
The vice-president of the United States of America, J.D. Vance, recently suggested that his country is no longer at war with Iran. This is the latest instance of linguistic gymnastics by the Donald Trump administration regarding a deeply unpopular conflict. Mr Vance based his argument on the US focus on economic sanctions against Iran — as opposed to military assaults — to pressure Tehran. Yet, both before and after his comments, the US and Iran engaged in active military hostilities, targeting each other’s ships, tankers and strategic facilities. A wedding in Iran was bombed, leaving at least five people dead and dozens injured. Iran continues to target US allies in the region, firing missiles this past week at Jordan, Kuwait and Bahrain. And the US president has threatened military escalation against Iran time and again. These are tell-tale signs of a slow-burn war, one in which the protagonists choose to turn the heat up or down when it suits them, on a weekly, daily, or even hourly basis. While they do not really know what they are cooking up anymore, neither side is willing to extinguish the flame yet.

This is a recipe for continued disaster — for the countries directly involved as well as the rest of the world. For Mr Trump’s team, the calculation appears to be to wait until the mid-term elections in November before any major escalation because his Republican Party faces major headwinds over public anger against the war. But even the most powerful military in history cannot dictate the direction of a war by itself; the conflict in Iran has shown this. Iran, too, will choose if and when it wants to amplify pressure on the US. The markets know this, that is why they remain in flux and why oil prices are, once again, edging close to a hundred dollars per barrel. Fuel prices across the world, including in India, remain high. Food and fertiliser prices have risen too and show no signs of coming down. The livelihoods of millions of Indians in the Gulf — as well as expatriates from other countries — hang in the balance. Mr Trump’s tactic of amplifying economic pressure on Iran by also punishing countries that trade with Tehran is further stressing the economies of the Global South, including India. Ultimately, a war in limbo means a world that is forced to stay in limbo. That is unacceptable. No amount of wordplay can alter that reality.

editorials.title: BRICS and its economic contradictions
editorials.passage:
The 2026 BRICS summit is all set to take place in New Delhi from September 11 to 13. BRICS has expanded its membership and now represents a larger share of the global economy in PPP (purchasing power parity) terms than the G7. Member-countries describe the bloc as a forum for multipolarity and shared prosperity. However, despite the carefully managed proclamations, something odd is going on. Intentionally or otherwise, BRICS countries are causing inflation, losses of export revenues, and growth stagnation to their partners. It would unfair though, to not mention what the BRICS has built. For instance, its $100-billion Contingent Reserve Arrangement (CRA), established in 2014, provides balance-of-payments support during financial stress. But the CRA does not monitor or coordinate the currency, commodity and inflation spillovers members impose on one another. BRICS therefore has crisis-response tools but no comparable surveillance mechanism.

Nearly two decades on, BRICS has no common mechanism for members to flag or discuss economic damage arising from another member’s policies. So, it has ended up as an ‘economic family’ without the ‘family spirit’ needed for solidarity. The consequences of this institutional gap are already visible in how members’ domestic economic decisions spill across BRICS borders.

One example is China’s management of the yuan to support exports. The yuan has weakened repeatedly during periods of economic stress, including during the 2018-19 US-China trade war. Such depreciation affects Indian and Brazilian manufacturers competing in the same markets. By contrast, the European Union has institutional forums through which cross-border monetary effects can at least be acknowledged and debated; BRICS has no equivalent mechanism. While a currency devaluation transmits cost shocks through exchange rates, commodity overlap transmits them directly through the global price of identical goods. Among the members of BRICS+, several major exporters compete in overlapping markets. This creates structural conflicts of interest among members in their export strategies, as illustrated in the Table.

This contradiction became evident when Saudi Arabia and the UAE joined BRICS in 2024, making the group home to three major oil producers. The discounted oil offered by Russia since 2022 is illustrative of how one member can defend market share at the cost of another. This spillover can also work in the other direction via imports between members. India imports up to $132 billion of goods a year from China, which is a major channel for the Chinese cost pressures to enter the Indian economy.

Rising production costs in China, whether due to wages, energy or supply disruptions, can increase costs for Indian importers, which can trickle down to domestic prices. But BRICS has not measured nor addressed these externalities of inflation. These asymmetries are not unique to China, but occur wherever a member of the BRICs has a significant economic size imbalance and trade dependence. These coordination gaps are more significant when considering the efforts to increase trade and settlement in members’ national currencies.

De-dollarisation is sometimes described as a route to financial freedom. However, it can also give rise to new financial fragilities, unless robust institutions are in place. Despite the distortions associated with dollar dominance, deep dollar markets have historically reduced some of the exchange-rate frictions involved in international trade. Greater use of national currencies, however, exposes trade to thinner bilateral currency markets. Currency pairs characterised by low trading volumes, limited liquidity, and wide bid-ask spreads, such as rupee/rouble, tend to experience greater exchange-rate volatility.

In the absence of deep and liquid foreign-exchange markets, economic shocks are more likely to generate sharp currency fluctuations, increasing uncertainty for traders and investors. As a result, inflationary and other macroeconomic shocks originating in one member economy can be transmitted more unevenly and with greater intensity to its trading partners. The argument, therefore, is not against local-currency trade; it is against pursuing de-dollarisation without the monetary coordination needed to manage its spillovers. The dollar meanwhile still accounts for roughly 47-49 per cent of SWIFT-processed payments, illustrating the scale that alternative settlement systems must still match.

Economic spillovers are not unique to BRICS; inflation, exchange rates, commodity prices and monetary policies inevitably cross borders. The real difference is that successful economic groupings eventually built institutions to manage them. The EU developed monetary coordination, while ASEAN+3 created mechanisms for macroeconomic surveillance and dialogue. BRICS was not meant to be an economic union at all but to be a sovereign driven diplomatic bloc that aims to seek a more multipolar world. That was a design which allowed for political cooperation without any deep economic coordination. This creates increasing economic interdependence, but no institutions to control costs.

But the solution to these problems does not merely involve the creation of a BRICS central bank, a common currency, or even any diminution of national sovereignty. What it does involve is a realisation that economic interdependence is both a source of opportunity and obligation. ASEAN+3’s Economic Review and Policy Dialogue offers a workable model, a macroeconomic surveillance without requiring members to surrender monetary sovereignty. BRICS could attach a comparable function to its existing finance ministers’ track. It could begin with a non-binding annual spillover report tracking how members’ currency, commodity and trade decisions affect one another. Such consultation and spillover monitoring would help members anticipate and manage the costs they impose on one another. Closing this gap will not come from reducing reliance on Western institutions, but from finally building the coordination machinery.

The writer is doctoral student in management, National Institute of Technology Rourkela

Published on September 8, 2026

editorials.title: Can data centres justify resources they consume?
editorials.passage:
Global tech companies are set to invest nearly $60 billion in AI-driven data centres over the next few years, with States competing aggressively through subsidised land, power, water, fiscal incentives and faster approvals. Uttar Pradesh’s new Data Centre Policy targets over ₹2 lakh crore in investments, while Andhra Pradesh and Telangana are emerging as strong challengers to established hubs.

By 2030, Maharashtra is expected to remain the largest market with 4,376 MW of capacity, followed by Andhra Pradesh (2,753 MW) and Telangana (1,926 MW). The Centre has proposed a tax holiday till 2047 for eligible foreign cloud companies using Indian data centres to serve overseas customers.

This enthusiasm is understandable. AI will need computing infrastructure. But before we celebrate every new data centre announcement, we must undertake a cost-benefit and risk analysis: what do we eventually gain?

Today, almost every critical component inside an AI data centre — GPUs, servers, networking equipment, storage systems and cooling infrastructure — is imported. The intellectual property belongs to global companies. India provides the land, electricity, data, water and incentives, while much of the value creation happens elsewhere.

Unlike factories or IT campuses, data centres are not large job creators. Construction generates employment for civil works, electrical installation and engineering, but once operational these facilities are highly automated. They require relatively small teams to manage servers, cooling systems, security and maintenance. We therefore create some construction activity, a few permanent jobs and while the high-value addition remains overseas.

Is this the right model fit for a country with India’s unique demographic and economic needs?

India is attractive because it offers abundant land, competitive construction costs, renewable energy potential and a rapidly growing AI market. But if our critical digital infrastructure increasingly runs on AWS, Google Cloud or Azure, our hospitals, banks, government platforms and AI applications also become dependent on foreign technology platforms and their commercial decisions.

There is another issue that deserves greater attention. AI data centres are resource intensive. A gigawatt-scale facility can consume as much electricity as a mid-sized Indian city, besides requiring substantial water for cooling.

When States commit renewable power and scarce water resources to these projects, we must ask whether the broader economic returns justify the public investment. The Ministry of Power estimates that AI data centres could add 26.3 GW of electricity load by 2031-32, equivalent to nearly 7 per cent of India’s entire projected peak demand. A country still working to guarantee reliable power to every home and factory is simultaneously being set to power the world’s AI ambitions. We need to look at the big picture holistically. What we need is a due consideration on the physical constraints of compute coupled with the implications.

Every major AI data centre should be assessed not only for its financial investment but also for its environmental and social impact. Electricity demand, water availability, cooling technologies, land use, biodiversity and waste generation should all be evaluated before incentives are granted. Equally important is understanding who bears the costs and who receives the benefits. A project may consume only a small share of a State’s water resources, yet place enormous pressure on a local watershed shared by farmers, households and industry.

More importantly, India must ensure that these investments create domestic capabilities.

Data centres should not become another industry where India supplies the land and electricity while the value chain remains offshore. Companies benefiting from subsidised land, power and tax incentives should also be required to create local value. States should negotiate that 30-40 per cent of equipment be sourced from Indian manufacturers, similar to local content requirements in defence and telecom which would help build domestic capabilities in servers, power systems, networking equipment, cooling technologies and electronics.

Alternatively an offset model could be an option. We must define the environmental and social guardrails — and the trade-offs we are prepared to accept.

Finally, we should recognise that computing itself is evolving rapidly. Today’s hyperscale AI data centres may not remain the dominant architecture forever. Quantum computing, edge AI and quantum-classical hybrid systems could dramatically reduce future computing, power and cooling requirements. India should therefore invest not only in data centres, but also in the hardware, software, semiconductors and products that will power the next generation of computing.

The writer is Co-founder of HCL, Chairman MGB (Mission Governing Board), National Quantum Mission and Chairman, IAIRO (Indian AI Research Organisation)

Published on September 8, 2026

editorials.title: Data centre expansion
editorials.passage:
A few months ago, I stood on a windswept plot near Tirunelveli, watching turbine blades turn against a clear southern sky, and found myself doing an odd calculation in my head: this one stretch of Tamil Nadu’s wind corridor could power a mid-sized AI campus round the clock, and nobody outside the State’s industrial circles seemed to have noticed. That gap — between what the south has quietly built and what the rest of India assumes lives only in Mumbai and Bengaluru — is, I’d argue, the most underpriced opportunity in Indian infrastructure today.

India generates nearly a fifth of the world’s digital data but holds barely 3 per cent of global data centre capacity. Capacity is doubling every three years, crossing 1.8 GW now and headed for 6.5 GW by 2030. Every CEO I know in this space is chasing the same three cities. I think that’s a mistake.

Chennai already commands 21 per cent of India’s data centre capacity, riding subsea cable landings like the India-Asia-Xpress, which brings in over 200 Tbps. That’s the headline everyone quotes. What gets missed is what sits behind Chennai — a 600-kilometre industrial spine running through Coimbatore, Madurai, Tiruchirapalli and Tirunelveli, with power, land and skilled labour already in place, waiting for someone to connect the dots.

I’ve sat across the table from State industrial officials in SIPCOT parks who can turn around power connections and land approvals in weeks, not the quarters it takes elsewhere. That execution speed matters more than people realise when a hyperscaler wants shovels in the ground within a fiscal year.

Here’s the part that should matter most to any CFO signing off on a campus: AI-density racks running 30-50 kW need serious, reliable, round-the-clock renewable power, not diesel gensets propping up a green PPA on paper. Tamil Nadu has been India’s wind capital for over three decades — Tirunelveli, Tuticorin, and Kanyakumari sit in one of the country’s strongest wind belts, paired with abundant solar in the interior districts. Layer in battery storage, and the southern corridor can credibly hit the 80 per cent-plus renewable run rate that separates a defensible green data centre from a greenwashed one. Compare that to retrofitting renewable infrastructure around an already-saturated Mumbai grid. One is building sustainability in from day one; the other is bolting it on. I know which balance sheet I’d rather defend to an ESG committee five years from now.

If I were allocating capital today, I wouldn’t chase another hyperscale campus in Mumbai’s crowded corridor. I’d back a distributed southern network: a Tier-4 anchor facility near Chennai for hyperscaler workloads, 10-20 MW edge nodes in Coimbatore and Madurai serving 5G and local enterprise demand, and — this is the part most operators skip — co-located wind and solar assets in Tirunelveli and Tuticorin feeding it all directly, with L&T-grade EPC execution and a genuine circular-construction discipline: green steel, low-carbon concrete, water-positive design from the first drawing.

Players like AdaniConneX, Yotta and STT GDC already understand the north-south imbalance. The ones who move first into Tamil Nadu’s southern districts, rather than fighting for the last available acre in Mumbai, will own the cost curve for the next decade.

By 2030, this sector will have absorbed $80-100 billion in capital and created over 100,000 direct engineering jobs, with another 300,000 indirect roles across construction and manufacturing. Someone will anchor the 10-12 GW of new renewable capacity that all this compute demands. I’d rather that anchor sit in Tirunelveli’s wind belt than in a congested coastal grid running on borrowed margin.

Data centres are no longer a niche real estate play — they’re becoming India’s next core utility. The operators who win won’t just be the fastest to build. They’ll be the ones who read the map correctly, and Tamil Nadu’s southern districts are, I think, the most under-read line on it.

The writer is President, Danfoss India, and Chairman, CII Southern Region

Published on September 8, 2026

editorials.title: AI equaliser for mid-sized firms
editorials.passage: Imagine a mid-sized Indian company employing 2,500 people. It designs and manufactures interiors and undertakes customised fit-outs for campuses, universities, student hostels, hotels, and hospitals. Each project involves drawings, specifications, bills of materials, quotations, procurement, manufacturing, installation, and after-sales service. ALSO READAfter the arbitrage The company has already experimented with AI and found several promising uses. Its CEO now faces a different question: should it keep buying AI as a service, or build a private AI capability of its own? That is becoming increasingly practical. Open-weight models such as Qwen, a family of large language models released by Chinese technology company Alibaba, can be downloaded and operated by the company itself. Unlike a proprietary model accessed as an external service, this one can run on infrastructure the enterprise controls. The company does not own the intellectual property in Qwen, but subject to its licence, it can operate a copy without sending every request to the model’s developer. Think of it as installing an AI engine inside the company. Employees would access a simple internal application, call it Company AI, using their normal corporate login. Behind it sits an open model, connected with appropriate permissions to the company’s existing information and systems. Suppose a salesperson is preparing a proposal for furnishing a 2,000-room student hostel. The system can retrieve specifications from previous projects, approved product catalogues, current prices, and relevant design standards, then help draft the proposal. An engineer might upload an architect’s specification and ask it to identify matching products. Procurement could compare a bill of materials against supplier data. Separately, a project manager could ask which components for a hospital installation are delayed. Customer service could retrieve maintenance instructions for a chair installed three years ago. The model supplies language and reasoning. The company’s own systems supply the facts. The competitive advantage does not lie primarily in owning the model. Models will improve and can be replaced. The harder asset to reproduce is the company’s accumulated knowledge: completed projects, pricing histories, drawings, supplier performance, and the judgement embedded in past decisions. There is, however, an unglamorous prerequisite: the facts need to be usable. Drawings live in one system, quotations in spreadsheets and email, specifications in inconsistently named PDFs, and valuable knowledge in the heads of experienced employees. Before connecting AI to everything, the CEO must invest in data plumbing. File naming needs standardisation. Product master files need a reliable home. Old drawings and project records need to be searchable. Versions must be controlled. Legacy paper archives containing useful technical knowledge may need digitisation. Retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, allows the model to retrieve relevant information from company records before producing an answer. But retrieval cannot repair bad source data. If three versions of a drawing exist and nobody knows which is current, AI merely makes the confusion easier to access. In manufacturing, an obsolete specification can turn into wrong procurement, wasted material, or a costly installation error. Next comes infrastructure. Running a capable open-weight model privately does not necessarily require a massive server farm. The company could operate dedicated GPUs on premise, use a private cloud environment, or ask a systems integrator to manage dedicated infrastructure. The choice depends on workload, cost, and data sensitivity. The important point is control. The company should know where its data goes, who can access it, what is logged, and which systems the model can touch. Security therefore cannot be bolted on later. Company AI should inherit the permissions employees already have. A salesperson should not suddenly gain access to supplier negotiations because an AI assistant can search them. Procurement should not see executive compensation. A project team working for one client may need to be prevented from retrieving another client’s confidential drawings. The principle is simple: employees see only what they are authorised to see. The company should also resist the temptation to automate everything immediately. AI can draft a quotation, flag inconsistencies, or prepare a comparison. It should not silently approve a commercial bid, change an engineering specification, or issue a purchase order merely because it can.
